citations.quote: Therefore, the oral health status of the patient, as well as their values and preferences and any information provided by their cardiac team, should be taken into account when considering antibiotic prophylaxis for procedures that involve manipulation of the gingival or periapical region of the teeth.
citations.source: SDCEP Antibiotic Prophylaxis (2026), 'At-risk' dental procedures

citations.quote: When treatment planning for a high risk patient who has chosen antibiotic prophylaxis for 'at-risk' dental procedures, consider carrying out multiple 'at-risk' procedures at the same visit (e.g. some periodontal indices, PMPR and subgingival restorations) to reduce the number of instances that the patient will need to take antibiotic prophylaxis.
citations.source: SDCEP Antibiotic Prophylaxis (2026), 'At-risk' dental procedures

firstPrinciples.title: Bisphosphonates persist in bone for years, so MRONJ risk does not reset when the drug is stopped
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Bisphosphonates bind hydroxyapatite and stay in the skeleton long after dosing stops. A drug holiday or completed course does not return the bone to its pre-drug state.
firstPrinciples.body:
## High affinity for hydroxyapatite

Bisphosphonates are skeleton-seeking. They bind hydroxyapatite at sites of bone remodelling, and once incorporated they stay there. Alendronate, the most common oral bisphosphonate, has a half-life in bone of around 10 years [1]. That number is for the drug in bone, not the drug in plasma — plasma half-life is short, but the depot in the skeleton is what matters for jaw biology.

## Why this matters at the chair

Because the drug remains active in bone, MRONJ risk persists after the patient stops taking the tablets. SDCEP therefore tells dentists that any patient who has taken bisphosphonates at any time in the past should be allocated to a risk group as if they are still taking the drug [2]. A drug holiday started by the prescriber, a completed five-year course, or a discontinued course because of side effects all leave the same residual risk. The clinician should not relax the protocol because the patient says they 'finished the tablets last year'.

## Contrast with denosumab

Denosumab is not stored in bone in the same way. Its effect on bone turnover diminishes within nine months of stopping treatment [3]. So for denosumab, historical use beyond nine months is no longer relevant, while for bisphosphonates 'past use' has no expiry.

citations.quote: The drugs have a high affinity for hydroxyapatite and persist in the skeletal tissue for a significant period of time, with alendronate having a half-life in bone of around 10 years.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 2.2 Bisphosphonates

citations.quote: If a patient has taken bisphosphonates in the past, allocate them to a risk group as if they are still taking the drugs.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 3 Risk Assessment

citations.quote: The effect of denosumab on bone turnover diminishes within nine months of treatment completion.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 3 Previous Treatment with Anti-resorptive or Anti-angiogenic Drugs

firstPrinciples.title: The jaw remodels faster than other bones, which is why anti-resorptives produce necrosis there specifically
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Bisphosphonates and denosumab suppress bone turnover throughout the skeleton, but the mandible and maxilla remodel at a higher baseline rate, so they suffer first when osteoclast activity is shut down.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A site-specific vulnerability

MRONJ does not happen in the femur or the spine. It happens in the jaw. SDCEP attributes this to the fact that the jaw has an increased remodelling rate compared to other skeletal sites, and the viability of bone in this region may therefore be adversely affected by drugs that suppress resorption [1]. When osteoclast activity is shut down across the whole skeleton, the bones that depend most on continuous turnover for vitality are hit hardest.

## Why dentists need this fact

This is the mechanistic justification for everything else in the guidance. It explains why oral surgery, periodontal procedures, and even mucosal trauma from a denture can tip a quietly suppressed jaw into frank necrosis. It also explains why the same drug, in the same dose, does not cause necrosis at non-jaw sites, and why fragility-fracture protection elsewhere in the skeleton remains a net benefit. The dentist's job is to minimise the local insults — extractions, ill-fitting prostheses, untreated periodontal disease — that the drug-suppressed jaw can no longer recover from at its usual pace.

## Soft-tissue and angiogenic side effects compound the problem

SDCEP also notes speculation that bisphosphonates inhibit soft-tissue cell proliferation, increase apoptosis, and impair angiogenesis [2]. So when a socket fails to heal at 8 weeks, both the bone and the overlying mucosa are working against the clinician.

citations.quote: The jaw is known to have an increased remodelling rate compared to other skeletal sites and therefore the viability of bone in this region may be adversely affected by the action of these drugs.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 2.2 Anti-resorptive Drugs

citations.quote: It is speculated that the bisphosphonates may also have an adverse effect on soft tissue cells by inhibiting proliferation and increasing apoptosis, which may lead to delayed soft tissue healing. There is also some evidence that these drugs can inhibit angiogenesis.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 2.2 Bisphosphonates

firstPrinciples.title: Cumulative dose, not current dose, drives MRONJ risk in bisphosphonate users
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Because bisphosphonates accumulate in bone, the longer a patient takes them and the higher the cumulative load, the greater the MRONJ risk. Duration crosses categories at five years for non-malignant disease.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Risk rises with exposure

The risk of MRONJ in patients on bisphosphonates is thought to increase as the cumulative dose increases, a direct consequence of the long half-life of the drug class [1]. This is why high-dose intravenous regimens used for solid-tumour bone metastases or multiple myeloma carry a much higher MRONJ risk than the lower-dose oral regimens used for osteoporosis. It also explains the specific finding that prevalence of MRONJ is higher in patients who have taken oral bisphosphonates for more than four years compared to those who have taken them for less [2].

## How this becomes a clinical rule

SDCEP turns this biology into a hard cut-off. A non-malignant disease patient on bisphosphonates for less than five years sits in the low risk group; cross five years and they are reclassified as higher risk [3]. The five years is anchored to the SIGN 142 recommendation that bisphosphonate therapy be reviewed at that point. The point for the dentist is that risk class is not static — it ratchets up with time on the drug, and the drug history must be re-taken at every recall.

## Cancer-dose patients are always higher risk

For cancer indications, dose intensity is high enough from the start that no time-on-drug threshold is needed; those patients are higher risk from day one.

citations.quote: The risk of MRONJ in patients being treated with bisphosphonate drugs is thought to increase as the cumulative dose of the drug increases, as a consequence of the long half-life of this drug class.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 3 Length of Bisphosphonate Treatment

citations.quote: one study finding a higher prevalence of MRONJ in patients who had taken oral bisphosphonates for more than four years compared to those who had taken the drugs for less than this time period.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 3 Length of Bisphosphonate Treatment

citations.quote: those patients who continue to take bisphosphonates after this five-year medication review are considered to be at higher risk of MRONJ and their risk level should be reclassified accordingly.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), section 3 Risk Categories

firstPrinciples.title: Absolute MRONJ risk is small, and the medication's benefit usually outweighs it
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Even in the highest-risk group, MRONJ risk is around 1 in 100. In osteoporosis patients it is closer to 1 in 1,000 or rarer. Stopping the drug does not remove the risk and may cost more than it saves.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The numbers

SDCEP frames MRONJ as a real but uncommon adverse effect. In cancer patients on anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic drugs, MRONJ risk is roughly 1% (range 0 to 2.3%), giving each patient about a 1 in 100 chance of developing the disease [1]. In patients on anti-resorptives for osteoporosis or other non-malignant bone disease, the risk is around 0.1% or less, putting it between 1 in 1,000 and 1 in 10,000 [2]. After tooth extraction specifically, incidence is estimated at 2.9% in cancer patients and 0.15% in osteoporosis patients [3].

## Why this matters for consent and counselling

The dentist's job is to put these numbers honestly to the patient without scaring them off either their medication or their dental treatment. SDCEP explicitly warns that the patient must not be discouraged from taking their anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic medication, because the disease being treated (osteoporosis fracture, metastatic bone pain) carries far greater absolute morbidity than MRONJ. The decision to start or stop the drug belongs to the prescribing physician, not the dentist.

## Stopping does not erase the risk

A further point worth communicating is that stopping bisphosphonates or denosumab does not eliminate MRONJ risk because of bone retention and the slow resolution of skeletal effects. So 'just come off the tablets' is not a safe shortcut to lower-risk dentistry.

citations.quote: For patients being treated with anti-resorptive or anti-angiogenic drugs for the management of cancer, the risk of MRONJ approximates 1% (range 0 – 2.3%), which suggests that each patient has a 1 in 100 chance of developing the disease.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), Appendix 4 Points to Cover During MRONJ Risk Discussion

citations.quote: For patients taking anti-resorptive drugs for the prevention or management of non-malignant disease (e.g. osteoporosis, Paget's disease), the risk of MRONJ approximates 0.1% or less, which suggests that each patient has between a 1 in 1000 and 1 in 10,000 chance of developing the disease.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), Appendix 4 Points to Cover During MRONJ Risk Discussion

citations.quote: The incidence of MRONJ after tooth extraction is estimated to be 2.9% in patients with cancer and 0.15% in patients being treated for osteoporosis.
citations.source: SDCEP MRONJ Guidance (2017, extant 2024), Appendix 4 Points to Cover During MRONJ Risk Discussion

firstPrinciples.title: Stopping the drug is usually more dangerous than the bleed
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Anticoagulants and antiplatelets exist to prevent strokes, MIs and thromboembolism. Dental bleeding is almost always controllable locally; thrombosis from interruption often is not.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The asymmetry the guidance is built on

SDCEP estimates the incidence of post-operative bleeding events requiring further haemostatic measures, after dental procedures in patients who continued their oral anticoagulant, at about 4%, with fewer than 0.1% needing hospitalisation [1]. Almost every reported bleed is controlled with sutures, packing and pressure. By contrast, an interrupted course of anticoagulation in the wrong patient — a metal valve, a recent stent, a recent PE — can produce a stroke or coronary thrombosis the dentist can do nothing about. That is why the guidance reads as it does: continue the drug, contain the wound, and reach for local measures first.

## What this means at the chair

The default for warfarin (INR <4), DOACs at low-risk procedures, prophylactic-dose LMWH and any antiplatelet (single or dual) is do not interrupt [2]. Even for higher-risk DOAC procedures, the modification is a single missed or delayed dose, exploiting the short half-life — not a stop. Three patient groups are absolute no-stop: prosthetic metal heart valves or coronary stents, PE or DVT in the last three months, and anticoagulation for cardioversion [3]. Interruption in those patients only happens on the cardiologist’s direct written instruction.

citations.quote: The incidence of post-operative bleeding events requiring further haemostatic measures, after dental procedures for patients who had continued their oral anticoagulant therapy perioperatively, has been estimated at approximately 4%. Notably, almost all bleeding events were managed with local haemostatic measures and less than 0.1% of patients continuing their anticoagulant required hospitalisation for treatment.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 3 Assessing Bleeding Risk

citations.quote: For a patient who is taking single or dual antiplatelet drugs, treat without interrupting their antiplatelet medication. (Strong recommendation; low certainty evidence)
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 8 Treating a Patient Taking an Antiplatelet Drug(s)

citations.quote: Do not interrupt anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy, except under direct written instruction from the patient’s cardiologist, for: patients with prosthetic metal heart valves or coronary stents; patients who have had a pulmonary embolism or deep vein thrombosis in the last three months; patients on anticoagulant therapy for cardioversion.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 4.4 General Advice for Managing Bleeding Risk

firstPrinciples.title: Half-life dictates the management strategy
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Warfarin acts for days, DOACs and LMWHs act for hours. The size of the time window is what determines whether you skip a dose or check an INR.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why the strategies look different

Warfarin has a long half-life, so an interruption leaves the patient sub-therapeutic for days, with a meaningful thromboembolic window. The right control variable for warfarin is therefore the INR, measured close to the procedure, not the dose [1]. DOACs are the opposite case: rapid onset of one to four hours and short half-lives of roughly five to eighteen hours [2]. That short window is what makes a single missed or delayed dose a viable option for higher-risk procedures, and why restart timing is measured in hours from haemostasis rather than days [3]. LMWHs behave more like the DOACs, which is why a recent dose stopped 24 hours previously is usually irrelevant by the time of dental treatment.

## The clinical translation

For warfarin, never stop, but verify INR is below 4; for DOACs at higher-risk procedures, miss apixaban or dabigatran or delay rivaroxaban or edoxaban; for LMWHs, identify whether the dose is prophylactic (continue) or treatment (consult). The drug-specific rule is always a downstream consequence of how long the drug acts.

citations.quote: Due to the longer half-life of warfarin, interrupting therapy would potentially leave the patient at sub-therapeutic levels of anticoagulation for longer than interruption of a DOAC.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 6 Treating a Patient Taking Warfarin or Another Vitamin K Antagonist

citations.quote: Compared to warfarin, the DOACs exhibit a rapid onset of action (1-4 hours) and have relatively short half-lives (5-13 hours for rivaroxaban, ~12 hours for apixaban, ~10-14 hours for edoxaban and ~13-18 hours for dabigatran, depending on renal function and age).
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 5 Treating a Patient Taking a Direct Oral Anticoagulant

citations.quote: Due to the short half-lives of the DOACs this will significantly reduce the level of anticoagulation at the time of dental treatment. The brief interruption and rapid onset of action of the DOACs when restarting reduces the period that the patient could be at sub-therapeutic anticoagulation levels and minimises the effect on thromboembolic risk.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 5.2 Management for Procedures with a Higher Risk of Bleeding Complications

firstPrinciples.title: Bleeding risk is the product of three multipliers, not just the drug
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Procedure invasiveness, drug regimen, and patient co-morbidities and co-medications all stack. Risk is multiplicative, so each layer must be looked at before deciding management.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Three independent risk multipliers

SDCEP separates the bleeding-risk question into three pieces: which procedure, which drug regimen, and which patient. Procedure risk is fixed by the operation — a six-point perio chart and a flap-raising surgical extraction sit at opposite ends [1]. Drug risk rises with combinations: dual antiplatelet therapy carries a higher peri- and post-operative bleeding risk than monotherapy [2]. Patient risk loads in extra factors that the dentist could otherwise miss: chronic renal failure, liver disease, haematological malignancy, recent chemotherapy, advanced heart failure, inherited bleeding disorders, and platelet disorders all push bleeding risk up independently of the prescribed anticoagulant [3]. Common drug groups including NSAIDs, SSRIs, SNRIs and herbals such as St John’s Wort, Ginkgo biloba and garlic add a further layer.

## Why the three-step assessment matters

Missing any of the three layers misclassifies the patient. The point of asking specifically about non-prescribed aspirin, kidney and liver disease, and bleeding history is that these change a low-risk procedure into a higher-risk one without changing the prescribed regimen. The management decision is made once all three multipliers are visible.

citations.quote: Dental procedures that are likely to result in bleeding are further categorised in Table 1 into those with a low risk of post-operative bleeding complications and those that are judged to be more invasive and potentially carry a relatively higher risk of bleeding complications.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 3.1 Which Dental Procedures Have the Highest Bleeding Risk?

citations.quote: Patients who are on dual or combination therapies and are taking more than one anticoagulant or antiplatelet drug are likely to have a higher bleeding risk than those on single drug therapies. Indeed, direct comparisons of dual versus single antiplatelet therapy suggest that the risks of both peri-operative and post-operative bleeding with minor oral surgery are higher for patients on dual therapy.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 3.2.1 Bleeding risks associated with different anticoagulants and antiplatelet drugs

citations.quote: Certain medical conditions are known to be associated with an increased bleeding risk, due to effects on either coagulation or platelet function, and should be taken into consideration when planning dental treatment for any patient. These include liver, kidney and bone marrow disorders.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 3.2.2 Bleeding risks associated with other medical conditions

firstPrinciples.title: Local haemostasis is the workhorse
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Almost all bleeding from dental procedures in anticoagulated patients can be controlled locally. Sutures, packing and pressure are the levers that make continuing the drug safe.
firstPrinciples.body:
## What local haemostasis actually controls

The arrest of bleeding is described by SDCEP as a core skill for primary dental care, with the practitioner expected to have absorbent gauze, haemostatic packing material such as oxidised cellulose or collagen sponge, and a suture kit on hand [1]. Suturing stabilises the clot, packing material and wound margins, while haemostatic packs encourage clot formation in the socket [2]. Across procedures and drug groups, the SDCEP recommendations end with the same instruction: achieve haemostasis with local measures before discharging the patient, and strongly consider suturing and packing, especially when travel time to emergency care is long [3].

## Why this is the lynchpin

The entire continue-the-drug strategy depends on local haemostasis being reliable. Tranexamic acid mouthwash adds little above good local technique and is not part of the standard primary-care kit in this guidance. Asking about non-animal-based products is part of routine consent. The corollary is that a clinician who is not confident in suturing and packing should not be doing higher-risk procedures on these patients in primary care without an experienced colleague involved.

citations.quote: The arrest of bleeding is a core skill for primary dental care and the dental practitioner should have the necessary equipment and skills to perform appropriate local haemostatic measures competently for dental procedures likely to cause bleeding. These include packing any open sockets with haemostatic material and placing sutures.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 4.1 Haemostatic Measures

citations.quote: Suturing may be used to stabilise the clot, packing material and wound margins, unless it is likely to cause further trauma.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 4.1 Haemostatic Measures

citations.quote: For all patients taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet drugs, haemostasis should be achieved using local measures prior to the patient being discharged from care. Serious consideration should be given to suturing and packing, taking into account all relevant patient factors.
citations.source: SDCEP Anticoagulants/Antiplatelets, Section 4.1 Haemostatic Measures

firstPrinciples.title: Amalgam restriction is environmental, not toxicological
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Article 10(2) restricts amalgam in children and pregnant or breastfeeding patients to cut mercury reaching the environment, not because amalgam fillings have been shown to harm patients.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The driver is Minamata, not patient toxicity

The phasing down of dental amalgam is a legal requirement under EU Regulation 2017/852, which ratifies the Minamata Convention on Mercury. The Convention's stated objective is reducing environmental mercury pollution, with the trade and supply of mercury cut by preventing its unnecessary use in products [1]. Dental amalgam was a target because it was estimated to account for 20 to 30 percent of EU mercury demand in 2010 [2].

## Patient-level evidence does not show harm

Independent reviews from COT, SCENIHR and the FDA all reached the same conclusion: there is no evidence that mercury exposure from amalgam restorations causes adverse health effects, in studies that included children, pregnant and breastfeeding women [3]. Placement and removal cause transient rises in plasma mercury, but these have not been shown to affect health [3].

## Why the restriction still focuses on children and pregnancy

The regulation does not explain its choice of groups, but the SDCEP advice notes that developing foetuses, infants and children are more susceptible to the toxic effects of other forms of mercury, so the targeting is best read as the precautionary principle of avoiding even theoretical risk [4]. Restricting use in children also produces future generations of amalgam-free patients, which feeds back into the environmental goal.

citations.quote: The aim of the Convention is to reduce the trade and supply of mercury by preventing its unnecessary use in products and manufacturing processes, with the overall objective of reducing environmental mercury pollution and the risk to human health.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 1.1 The Minamata Convention on Mercury

citations.quote: Dental amalgam remains one of the most durable and cost-effective dental restorative materials and was estimated to account for 20-30% of the demand for mercury in the EU in 2010, with predictions that it will become the largest use as the mercury-cell based chlor-alkali industry is phased out.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 1.2 The Contribution of Dental Amalgam to Mercury Use and Environmental Pollution

citations.quote: Studies have indicated that the placement and removal of dental amalgam restorations leads to transiently elevated plasma levels of mercury but there is no evidence that this affects health.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 4.1 Safety of Dental Amalgam and Alternative Restorative Materials

citations.quote: While not explained in the EU regulation, since developing foetuses, infants and children are more susceptible to the toxic effects of other forms of mercury, it is likely that the targeting of children, pregnant and breastfeeding women in Article 10(2) reflects the precautionary principle of avoiding even theoretical risk.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 3 Advice on the Restrictions on the Use of Dental Amalgam

firstPrinciples.title: Methylmercury bioaccumulation links amalgam waste to human harm
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Elemental mercury from amalgam is biologically stable, but once released into the environment microbes convert it to methylmercury, which concentrates up the food chain into fish and ultimately people.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Two different forms of mercury

The elemental mercury inside set dental amalgam is a relatively stable form, and there is no evidence that it presents a direct health risk to a person carrying amalgam fillings [1]. The dangerous form is organic methylmercury, which is the most toxic and bioaccumulative species of mercury and is the main route by which the general population is actually exposed, through fish and other marine species [1].

## How amalgam connects to that route

The link between dental practice and dietary methylmercury exposure runs through the environment. Non-organic mercury released from amalgam, whether through manufacture, placement and removal, landfill, waste water, cremation or burial, can be converted to methylmercury by aquatic microorganisms once it reaches water, and then concentrates up the food chain [2]. Globally, around two thirds of the mercury contained in dental amalgam is eventually released into atmosphere, soil, surface or groundwater [3].

## Practical implication

This is why amalgam separators on dental units, careful waste handling and the broader phase-down all matter even though the filling in a patient's mouth is not the toxic form. The clinician's environmental footprint, not the patient's exposure, is the lever the legislation pulls on.

citations.quote: The main source of exposure to mercury for the general population is through the consumption of fish and other marine species contaminated with organic methylmercury, the most toxic and bioaccumulative form of mercury. The elemental mercury contained in dental amalgam is a more stable form and there is no evidence that it presents a direct health risk to individuals who have amalgam restorations.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 1.2 The Contribution of Dental Amalgam to Mercury Use and Environmental Pollution

citations.quote: non-organic forms of mercury, such as in dental amalgam, released into the environment can undergo conversion to methylmercury by aquatic microorganisms and become concentrated in the human food chain.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 1.2 The Contribution of Dental Amalgam to Mercury Use and Environmental Pollution

citations.quote: It has been estimated that globally around two-thirds of the mercury in dental amalgam is eventually released into the atmosphere, soil, surface and groundwater.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 1.2 The Contribution of Dental Amalgam to Mercury Use and Environmental Pollution

firstPrinciples.title: Alternative materials trade durability for adhesion and aesthetics
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Resin composite and glass-ionomer can replace amalgam in most clinical situations, but they need a dry field and bring different strengths, so the limit is technique-sensitivity, not material capability.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why amalgam was hard to displace

Amalgam is one of the most durable and cost-effective restorative materials, and the published evidence shows higher survival rates for amalgam than for resin composite in posterior permanent teeth [1]. Any phase-down therefore has to be defended on the basis that the alternatives, while different, are clinically adequate.

## What composite and glass-ionomer actually deliver

Posterior resin composite restorations can have acceptable survival rates and last for decades, with failure rates under 10 percent at 10 years [2]. Glass-ionomer is less wear resistant than amalgam, but offers adhesion and fluoride release, and one systematic review found higher caries-prevention outcomes at restoration margins compared with amalgam over six years [3].

## The real-world ceiling

The SDCEP working group identified two practical limits on alternatives: inability to obtain adequate moisture control, and inability to obtain patient cooperation for the time the procedure takes [4]. When either of those is missing, even a large or extensive cavity cannot be reliably restored with composite or glass-ionomer, and amalgam may still be the only feasible choice. This frames the exception clause in Article 10(2) as a clinical reality, not a loophole.

citations.quote: There is low quality evidence that suggests that resin composite restorations in permanent posterior teeth have higher failure rates and risk of secondary caries than dental amalgam.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 4.3 Effectiveness of Alternative Approaches and Materials

citations.quote: Nonetheless, the evidence indicates that resin composite restorations can exhibit substantial longevity, with failure rates of less than 10 percent after 10 years.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 4.3 Effectiveness of Alternative Approaches and Materials

citations.quote: Other evidence suggests that glass-ionomer cement has a higher caries-preventive effect for single surface restorations in permanent teeth after six years compared to dental amalgam, although no difference was found for primary teeth.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 4.3 Effectiveness of Alternative Approaches and Materials

citations.quote: the main limitations for the placement of alternative restorations are when it is not possible to obtain adequate moisture control or patient cooperation for the treatment required.
citations.source: SDCEP Dental Amalgam Implementation Advice, section 4.4 Rationale for the Advice

firstPrinciples.title: Primary teeth need different rules from permanent teeth
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: The dentition is transient but the permanent dentition has to last a lifetime. Treatment thresholds and goals shift accordingly between the two.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A finite lifespan changes the goal

A primary tooth is on a clock — first molars exfoliate around 9 to 11 years, second molars around 10 to 12. The aim of caries management is to get the tooth there without pain, infection or treatment-induced anxiety [1]. That is why slowing the disease, with techniques like Hall sealing, can be enough; full caries removal may not be required, and is in fact discouraged because the pulp-exposure risk is too high.

## The permanent dentition gets the harder push

For permanent teeth the goal flips: prevention and management have to maximise lifetime longevity. SDCEP is explicit that the personal care plan must prioritise keeping permanent molars caries-free, and that restorations should be done to the same high standard as for adults [2]. Sequencing follows the same logic — fissure-seal a first permanent molar before restoring a primary molar.

citations.quote: For a child with a carious lesion in a primary tooth, choose the least invasive, feasible caries management strategy, taking into account: the time to exfoliation, the site and extent of the lesion, the risk of pain or infection, the absence or presence of infection, preservation of tooth structure, the number of teeth affected, avoidance of treatment-induced anxiety.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Caries management in primary teeth (key recommendations)

citations.quote: When restoring permanent teeth in children, ensure this is done to the same high standard as for adults to maximise the longevity of restorations and to minimise the amount of treatment required later in life.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Caries management in permanent teeth

firstPrinciples.title: Sealing arrests caries by starving the biofilm
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Caries is a biofilm-driven disease. Cut off the substrate and oxygen supply and the biofilm changes its behaviour, regardless of how much carious dentine remains under the seal.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Why the Hall Technique works

The Hall Technique places a preformed metal crown over a carious primary molar with no caries removal, no preparation and no anaesthesia. It works because the crown completely seals the carious lesion from the oral environment, altering the ecosystem of the plaque biofilm enough to slow or even arrest caries progression [1]. The lesion no longer receives fermentable carbohydrate or fresh bacteria from saliva, so progression slows or stops.

## The seal is the active ingredient

The same logic underpins fissure sealing of initial occlusal lesions and resin infiltration of proximal lesions. SDCEP makes the consequence explicit: if the seal fails, caries will progress [2]. That is why active surveillance — checking sealants visually and with a probe at every recall, replacing worn ones — is non-negotiable. Sealing is not a one-off intervention; it is a maintained barrier.

citations.quote: To completely seal a carious lesion so that the environment of the plaque biofilm is altered sufficiently to slow or even arrest caries progression.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Hall Technique

citations.quote: No local anaesthesia, tooth preparation or caries removal is used and there is no risk of iatrogenic damage to adjacent teeth. This less invasive approach may be more technically feasible and acceptable in some situations, but it should be noted that regular surveillance of the sealant is required. If the seal fails, caries will progress.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Sealant/infiltration

firstPrinciples.title: Extracting an FPM at 8 to 10 lets the SPM take its place
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Interceptive extraction of a hopeless first permanent molar exploits the unerupted second permanent molar's drift potential. Get the timing right and the second molar fills the gap.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A narrow window of opportunity

If a first permanent molar (FPM) of poor prognosis is extracted between 8 and 10 years of age, the unerupted second permanent molar (SPM) is well placed to drift forward and erupt into the FPM space, allowing development of an acceptable, caries-free dentition without spacing [1]. Outside that window the gain is unpredictable.

## What needs to be true on the radiograph

The occlusal outcome depends on more than age. Favourable factors include class I incisor and molar relationships, mild or no buccal-segment crowding, second premolars and third molars present radiographically, distal angulation of the SPMs, and SPM bifurcation forming on the radiograph [2]. Mesial drift of the upper SPM is more predictable than the lower, so the lower arch is the one most tightly tied to the 8-10 year window.

## The clinical implication

For a child with an FPM that is going to be lost anyway — through MIH, advanced caries or recurrent disease — temporising it (often with a Hall-style PMC) until the optimal age is a legitimate plan. The FPM then comes out at the moment that maximises the chance of self-correction, rather than whenever pain forces the decision.

citations.quote: In some situations, interceptive extraction of FPMs of poor long-term prognosis at 8-10 years of age can allow unerupted SPMs to erupt into an acceptable position. This could facilitate the development of a caries free dentition in the patient, without spacing.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Management of FPMs of poor prognosis

citations.quote: Factors that might contribute to an optimal occlusal outcomes include: patient age; considered optimal between 8-10 years old but this is most relevant for the lower arch... class I incisor and molar relationships... mild buccal crowding or no buccal segment crowding/spacing; second premolars and third molars present on radiograph; distal angulation of the SPMs; bifurcation of SPMs forming on radiograph.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Management of FPMs of poor prognosis

firstPrinciples.title: Treatment-induced anxiety is itself a clinical outcome
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: How a child experiences early dental care shapes whether they return as an adult. Avoidable anxiety is treated as iatrogenic harm, not just a soft inconvenience.
firstPrinciples.body:
## A second outcome alongside the tooth

SDCEP repeatedly weights treatment decisions against the risk of causing anxiety. The aim is for the child to grow up feeling positive about their oral health and able to maintain it [1]. That is why minimally invasive techniques are preferred for primary teeth, why first-visit extractions are avoided where possible, and why a procedure is stopped if the child becomes distressed.

## The clinical mechanics

Distressing experiences — particularly traumatic LA, sleight-of-hand techniques, and forcing through resistance — can create long-lasting "mistrust" phobias that are difficult to resolve later [2]. The defensive moves are slow injection, topical first, distraction during LA, behaviour shaping, and a treatment compromise (e.g. fluoride varnish only) to end a faltering visit on a win. If the child resists, you stop, even if the parent disagrees.

citations.quote: to reduce the risk of the child experiencing pain or infection or acquiring treatment-induced dental anxiety if dental caries does occur; for the child to grow up feeling positive about their oral health and with the skills and motivation to maintain it.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Overarching principles

citations.quote: Most children will be apprehensive about receiving LA. However, the use of "sleight of hand" techniques when giving LA may lead to "mistrust" phobias, which may be difficult to resolve at a later time.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Local anaesthesia

firstPrinciples.title: Fluoride is dose-, frequency- and rinsing-sensitive
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Fluoride only protects the dentition while it is in contact with enamel. Concentration, frequency of application and what happens after brushing all change the effective dose.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The post-brush rule that doubles the effect

Children who spit but do not rinse after brushing experience significantly less caries than those who rinse with water [1]. The reason is simple: rinsing washes the fluoride straight off the teeth before it has done its work. The same logic underpins brushing last thing at night, when reduced salivary flow keeps fluoride in the mouth longer.

## Concentration is risk-stratified

Standard Prevention uses 1000-1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste twice daily. For children at increased risk, the concentration steps up: 1350-1500 ppm up to age 10, then prescribed 2800 ppm for ages 10-16 for a limited period, with regular review [2]. Professional fluoride varnish follows the same logic: twice a year for Standard Prevention, four times a year for Enhanced. Frequency, not bigger single hits, is what does the work.

citations.quote: Children who spit out and do not rinse after brushing experience significantly less caries compared with those who rinse their mouth out with water after brushing.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Toothbrushing

citations.quote: Recommend the use of 1350-1500 ppm fluoride toothpaste for children up to 10 years of age. Prescribe 2800 ppm fluoride toothpaste for children aged 10 - 16 years for a limited period (see SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry guidance for details). Regular review is required.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Toothbrushing (Enhanced Prevention)

firstPrinciples.title: Most child dental infection is fixed locally, not by antibiotics
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Antibiotics do not drain pus and do not remove the source. They are reserved for spreading or systemic infection, while the workhorse remains pulp/cavity access for drainage.
firstPrinciples.body:
## The default move is mechanical

The majority of dental infections in children can be managed by local measures, and antibiotics should not be first line unless there are signs or symptoms of systemic involvement, spreading infection, or the child is medically compromised [1]. For a primary tooth that means gentle hand excavation of carious tissue to open communication with the necrotic pulp chamber and let the abscess drain. For a permanent tooth it means accessing the pulp chamber to remove the necrotic pulp.

## When antibiotics are actually justified

Antibiotics enter the picture only when the infection is no longer localised. The triggers are spreading cellulitis, systemic symptoms (fever, malaise, lymphadenopathy) and the medically compromised host [2]. Even then they buy time for definitive treatment — extraction, pulpotomy or pulpectomy — which still has to happen.

citations.quote: The majority of dental infections can successfully be managed by local measures. Antibiotics should not be first line treatment unless there are signs/symptoms of systemic involvement, spreading infection and/or the child is medically compromised.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Local measures

citations.quote: Antibiotics are not recommended unless there are signs of spreading infection or systemic symptoms.
citations.source: SDCEP Prevention and Management of Dental Caries in Children, Pain or infection (Management)

firstPrinciples.title: Antibiotics treat spreading infection, not pain
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Dental abscess is a localised collection of pus that is cured by drainage and removing the cause; antibiotics serve only to control bacteria that have escaped local control.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Drainage cures the abscess

A dental abscess is fundamentally a mechanical problem. Pus inside the tooth is treated by extraction or by going through the root canals; pus in soft tissue is treated by incision and drainage [1]. Without drainage, no antibiotic course will sterilise a closed pus collection, because the drug cannot reach bacteria in the necrotic core in adequate concentration.

## Antibiotics are reserved for spread

Antibiotics are required only when local measures have failed or there is cellulitis, spreading infection, or systemic involvement [2]. They are not indicated in the absence of swelling or other signs of infection [3]. Prescribing for pain alone trains patients to expect antibiotics for toothache and contributes to resistance.

## Resistance is the bigger picture

The routine use of broad-spectrum antibiotics is associated with the rise in Clostridium difficile infection in primary and secondary care, which is why second-line drugs like clindamycin, co-amoxiclav and clarithromycin should be reserved for severe infection that has failed first-line treatment [4].

citations.quote: If pus is present in dental abscesses, drain by extraction of the tooth or through the root canals. If pus is present in any soft tissue, attempt to drain by incision.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Dental abscess: local measures

citations.quote: If local measures have proved ineffective or there is evidence of cellulitis, spreading infection or systemic involvement, one of the following first-line antibiotics can be used.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Dental abscess: first line antibiotics

citations.quote: Antibiotics are not indicated in the absence of swelling or other signs of infection.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Contraindications & cautions, general advice

citations.quote: The use of broad-spectrum antibiotics is associated with the increase in Clostridium difficile infection observed in both primary and secondary care.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Dental abscess: second line antibiotics

firstPrinciples.title: Paracetamol and ibuprofen alternated control most dental pain
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Acute dental pain has both inflammatory and nociceptive components, and combining a non-NSAID analgesic with an NSAID exploits separate pathways without exceeding either drug's safe ceiling.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Two drugs, two pathways

Most odontogenic pain is relieved effectively using paracetamol and/or ibuprofen [1]. Paracetamol acts centrally; ibuprofen reduces peripheral prostaglandin-driven inflammation. Either drug alone often falls short of the inflammatory pain produced by an irreversible pulpitis or a fresh extraction socket.

## Alternation, not addition of doses

Where paracetamol or ibuprofen alone is not effective, both can be given alternately — ibuprofen first then paracetamol two hours later, repeating using normal daily doses [2]. This controls ongoing pain and pyrexia without exceeding the maximum daily dose of either drug. The overall principle is optimal analgesia: the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration that controls symptoms [3].

## Safer than escalation to opioids

For a primary care dental setting, this combination usually outperforms higher-tier analgesia and avoids the side-effect profile of opioids. It also avoids the trap of doubling either drug, which raises hepatic risk for paracetamol and gastric and renal risk for ibuprofen.

citations.quote: Most odontogenic pain can be relieved effectively using paracetamol and/or ibuprofen to provide optimal analgesia.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Contraindications & cautions, general advice

citations.quote: In cases where paracetamol or ibuprofen alone is not effective, both paracetamol and ibuprofen can be given alternately (i.e. ibuprofen can be taken first and then paracetamol 2 hours later, and so on, using the normal daily doses given below). This regimen controls ongoing pain and pyrexia without exceeding the recommended dose or frequency of administration for either drug.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Analgesics

citations.quote: Optimal analgesia is defined as the lowest effective dose of painkillers taken for the shortest duration necessary to control symptoms without exceeding the maximum dose and taking into account the patient's age, weight and relevant health conditions.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Contraindications & cautions

firstPrinciples.title: Antifungal choice depends on the form and extent of candidosis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Oral candidosis presents in distinct clinical patterns, and the right treatment is set by which pattern is in front of you and how widespread it is, not by the diagnosis alone.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Form and extent set the agent

Mild and localised pseudomembranous or erythematous candidosis responds to topical miconazole oromucosal gel [1]. Severe or extensive infection, or topical failure, calls for systemic fluconazole [2]. The same logic applies to denture stomatitis: local measures usually suffice, miconazole gel applied to the fitting surface of the upper denture is an adjunct, and systemic fluconazole is not required routinely [3].

## Angular cheilitis splits along denture lines

In denture wearers, angular cheilitis is usually a fungal Candida infection with concurrent denture stomatitis; in non-denture wearers it is more likely staphylococcal [4]. Miconazole 2% cream covers both, which is why it is the default unless contraindicated; sodium fusidate ointment is reserved for clearly bacterial cases.

## Predisposing factors must be addressed too

Patients on inhaled corticosteroids should rinse and gargle after each inhaler use and use a spacer; diabetes, nutritional deficiency and immunocompromise should be managed or referred [5]. Without addressing these, recurrence is the rule and antifungal courses are wasted.

citations.quote: Miconazole oral gel is recommended for topical treatment of mild and localised infections.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Candidosis

citations.quote: Systemic antifungal treatment with fluconazole is appropriate for patients with severe or extensive infection or for whom topical treatment is unsuitable or ineffective, unless otherwise contraindicated.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Candidosis

citations.quote: Systemic antifungal agents (e.g. fluconazole) are not required routinely for the treatment of denture stomatitis.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Denture stomatitis

citations.quote: Angular cheilitis in denture-wearing patients is usually caused by a fungal infection with Candida spp. and there is an associated denture stomatitis that should be treated concurrently. In those without dentures, angular cheilitis is more likely to be caused by a a staphylococcal bacterial infection.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Angular cheilitis

citations.quote: Advise patients who use a corticosteroid inhaler that immediately after using the inhaler they should rinse their mouth and gargle with water and then spit the water out.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Candidosis: local measures

firstPrinciples.title: IM adrenaline is the only intervention that reverses anaphylaxis
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Anaphylaxis is a distributive shock with airway compromise, and adrenaline reverses both arms by alpha-driven vasoconstriction and beta-driven bronchodilation; antihistamines do neither.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Adrenaline by IM injection, weight-banded

Adult adrenaline is 0.5 ml of 1:1000 IM, repeated after 5 minutes if needed [1]. The paediatric doses follow age bands: 0.3 ml for 6 to 11 years, 0.15 ml for 6 months to 5 years, with the 12 to 17 year band on the adult dose unless the child is small or pre-pubertal. The reason this matters is that pre-filled patient autoinjectors such as EpiPens may contain less adrenaline than the recommended emergency dose [2], so practice ampoules and pre-filled syringes are stocked separately.

## Antihistamines are for mild allergy only

Mild allergy with urticaria, rhinitis or mild bronchospasm responds to oral cetirizine, chlorphenamine or loratadine. Severe reactions must be treated as anaphylaxis — antihistamines are insufficient because they cannot reverse vasodilation or laryngeal oedema [3].

## Oxygen and posture support physiology

While waiting for adrenaline to act and for the ambulance, lay the patient flat with feet raised to support venous return and blood pressure, and give 100% oxygen at 15 litres per minute. If cardiac arrest follows, basic life support and early defibrillation come next.

citations.quote: Administer adrenaline, 0.5 ml (1:1000), i.m. injection repeated after 5 minutes if needed.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Anaphylaxis

citations.quote: Note that pre-filled syringes are convenient in an emergency situation due to their ease of use but those provided for patient use (e.g. EpiPen® etc.) may contain less adrenaline than recommended for the management of medical emergencies.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Drugs for medical emergencies

citations.quote: Treatment with antihistamines is only suitable in cases of mild allergy; severe allergic reactions must be treated as anaphylaxis.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Mild allergic reactions

firstPrinciples.title: NSAID safety is decided by the patient, not the drug
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs share a predictable list of organ-system risks, and screening the patient for these risks before prescribing is what separates safe from harmful use.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Five recurring danger zones

NSAIDs cause trouble for patients with active or previous peptic ulcer disease, asthma in those whose attacks are triggered by NSAIDs, anticoagulation, severe heart failure, and severe renal or hepatic impairment [1]. Aspirin allergy or hypersensitivity is a hard contraindication for the whole class. Ibuprofen should be capped at 1200 mg per day in cardiovascular disease, hypertension, the elderly, and those on low-dose aspirin [2].

## Paracetamol fills the safety gap

When NSAIDs are unsafe, paracetamol is the analgesic of choice in pregnancy, breastfeeding, and patients on anticoagulants — it does not affect platelets or cause gastric bleeding [3]. In severe renal impairment paracetamol is still preferred but at a reduced dose with GMP liaison [4].

## Gastric protection is sometimes mandatory

Where an NSAID must be prescribed in someone with previous or active peptic ulcer disease, a proton pump inhibitor like lansoprazole or omeprazole is co-prescribed for the duration of the analgesic course [5]. The same applies in elderly patients with GI risk factors.

citations.quote: Avoid use in those with a hypersensitivity to aspirin or any other NSAID, including those in whom attacks of asthma, angioedema, urticaria or rhinitis have been precipitated by aspirin or any other NSAID. Do not prescribe for patients taking a low dose of aspirin daily. Avoid use in patients with previous or active peptic ulcer disease, unless a proton pump inhibitor is co-prescribed, and use with caution in the elderly, patients with allergic disorders, pregnant women, nursing mothers, those taking oral anticoagulants such as warfarin, those with coagulation defects, those with an inherited bleeding disorder, and those with renal, cardiac or hepatic impairment.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Ibuprofen

citations.quote: Prescribe ibuprofen up to 1200 mg per day as a first-line option (note that this is a lower dose than the 4 x 400 mg per day regimen recommended in the BNF for dental pain). For higher doses liaise with the patient's GMP.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Cardiac/circulatory conditions

citations.quote: For people taking anticoagulants paracetamol is considered safer than aspirin or NSAIDs because it does not affect platelets or cause gastric bleeding.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Bleeding tendencies

citations.quote: Prescribe paracetamol with caution to people with severe renal impairment. Dose reduction might be required; liaise with the patient's GMP to discuss.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Renal conditions

citations.quote: In patients who have a history of previous or active peptic ulcer disease where paracetamol alone is not sufficient for the treatment of odontogenic pain, and a NSAID (i.e. ibuprofen or diclofenac) is required, prescribe a proton pump inhibitor (i.e. lansoprazole and omeprazole) in conjunction with the NSAID.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Proton pump inhibitors

firstPrinciples.title: Metronidazole interacts hard with alcohol and warfarin
firstPrinciples.broaderContext: Metronidazole's pharmacology produces two unforgiving interactions in primary dental practice that the prescriber must hold in working memory before writing the script.
firstPrinciples.body:
## Disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol

Metronidazole has a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol, so patients must be advised to avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least 48 hours after stopping [1]. Symptoms include flushing, nausea, vomiting, palpitations and headache. Patients underestimate this — practical advice covers cooking sauces and over-the-counter cold remedies that contain alcohol.

## Absolute contraindication with warfarin

Metronidazole potentiates the anticoagulant effect of warfarin to a degree that the SDCEP guidance simply prohibits the combination [2]. For penicillins like phenoxymethylpenicillin and amoxicillin the recommendation is less absolute — the antibiotic potentially alters the anticoagulant effect, so the INR is checked 4 to 7 days after starting [3].

## Build a habit of asking before prescribing

The practical implication: before writing metronidazole, ask about alcohol intake and take a careful drug history. If the patient is on warfarin, switch to amoxicillin (with INR monitoring) or, in penicillin allergy, a second-line agent.

citations.quote: Advise patient to avoid alcohol during treatment and for at least 48 hours after stopping treatment (metronidazole has a disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol).
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Metronidazole

citations.quote: Do not prescribe metronidazole for patients taking warfarin.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Metronidazole

citations.quote: people taking warfarin, since phenoxymethylpenicillin or amoxicillin potentially alter the anticoagulant effect of warfarin. If either antibiotic is prescribed for patients taking warfarin, the INR should be checked 4-7 days after the antibiotic course has started.
citations.source: SDCEP Drug Prescribing for Dentistry, Contraindications & cautions - antibiotics
